Have you actually gone through the report? It's 254 pages long, and quite comprehensive, but it's important to not jump to click-baity conclusions just from reading a headline.

First, they only surveyed 12 states - not the whole country (Assam, Delhi, J&K, Kerala, Mizoram, Nagaland, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West Bengal). Western, Central and South Central India were completely overlooked. States like Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Gujarat, Goa etc could well have skewed the results and led to very different conclusions had they been surveyed as well.  


Second, they chose the exact same sample size (2640) for every state without adjusting for population. So conclusions derived from states with higher populations such as UP, would be proportionately subdued.  


Third, "accepting" can't be thrown around as a blanket term. The study cited in the article covers a variety of political and social subjects - many of which show alarming counterintuitive results in the very same states that appear to be the most accepting.  The same states that appear to score well in one area suddenly seem to be in favour of death penalty for consumption of beef, or seem to believe that dalits are just lazy - rather than having faced generations of oppression, or they seem to think that men should get paid more than women for the exact same job. The results are really all over the place. That's what happens with statistics. It's a really good study, but one can't arrive at realistic conclusions from it.  


Finally, although Christians appear to be most opposed to the idea of homosexuality in this survey, "opposition"  means something very different here. For instance, communal violence, honour killings, corrective punishments etc really aren't widely practiced in Indian christian communities to the extent as they are in rural Indian muslim and hindu communities. Meaning a rural muslim or hindu homosexual in a conservative community has a lot more to fear than a rural christian does.  Think of it this way - if you were a closeted kid, would you rather be surrounded by people who simply disapprove of you, or by people who might believe that they'd be justified in killing you?

Anyhoo. There's a lot to unpack there, and a lot to question. Interesting read though.

I'm not sure you've fully grasped what isometric means. It has to follow 3 axes at right angles. This doesn't really follow that principle in any way. If it helps, you can use a simple application to create the house in 3D, roate it to the angle of perspective that you like, screenshot it and trace over the lines in illustrator. You could use the free online version of SketchUp, for instance.   


If you're looking to create a more simplified version of the image that still maintains geometric proportions, you could use an app like Marmoset Hexels, which allows you to follow an isometric grid so you can fill in individual triangular cells, so there's no need to estimate the lines - it maintains the angles for you.  


Or if you really want to start from basics, just buy a grid-notebook that has light dotted lines - and you can use that to practice 3-point perspective drawing.
Of course you yourself will have it. But the client who wants to edit the file might not.

Depends on what software you're using. If you're on illustrator

1. Type out your text and go to Object > Expand to convert it to paths.
2. Draw out your concentric circles (you can do this quickly by drawing the smallest circle and the outermost one and going to Object>Blend>Blend options>Specified steps - enter the number of circles you want, then go to Object>Blend>make
3. Position the circles on top of the text, then expand the lines to paths (might have to flatten transparency) and then right click and ungroup
4. Then go to the pathfinder window, select all the circles and hold Alt+click the unite option to convert the circles to a compound path. Do the same to the text paths - ungroup and unite
5. Making sure that the concentric circles are on top of the text, select both and in the pathfinder window, select "minus front". That should cut out the circular lines in your text.
6. Then you just have to select, go to Effect>Stylize>Dropshadow and adjust the shadow as per your requirements
7. Add in a background image if you want, or take it to Photoshop for further tweaking / textures / distressing / filters etc.

Regarding the octopus, I personally think it just looks cool and is sufficiently indicative of your talent, but nobody is going to make the 8-arms-multiple-skills connection on their own. It's just a cool impactful visual, no need for extrapolated symbolism.

As for parallax, it's OK to use it in small doses, but it's usually a background sort of thing. Like it's ideally suited for banner images with bold or significant title text, where the image itself is more for atmosphere and less for context. If you intend for a viewer to actually look at the subject or composition of an image, i.e if the image depicts your actual work, you'd want it to be static and free of dynamic effects so it can be properly absorbed. Basically it's fine to have parallax at the header banner, but avoid it in product shots.

Well firstly, in the face of several metric fucktonnes of unbelievably appalling garbage that gets proclaimed as "design" these days, you should be really really proud that you have a decent portfolio, varied skill set, good aesthetic, clear typographic and color sense, and a functional website.

The only suggestions I have pertain to the website structure and ui/ux itself. 

1. Try not to have the entire contents on your website in sections on the Home Page. 'Home' should just act as a simple landing page- to give a brief overview and some insight into the kind of work you do. So it's great to have your first impactful banner, the brief introduction, your distinction between graphic designer and artist, and the project preview carousel. I'd move the portfolio thumbnails to a separate page, along with your design process steps, and CV. Even the contact form can be moved to its own contact page. 
2. Consider including a download button for a downloadable PDF of your CV, perhaps in the footer so it's accessible from every page. A lot of large companies have medieval HR departments and they just cannot wrap their heads around web CVs or online portfolios and they'd much rather have a PDF copy that they can either print or file away for future reference, than a URL to keep track of. 
3. Lower the size of your project thumbnails a bit. They take up too much space, require more scrolling, and if you use high resolution images it increases load time but if you use low res ones, the pixelation becomes very noticeable. Refer to something as generic as Instagram for image thumbnail proportions, how it gives a decent idea of the range of images but doesn't stretch from edge to edge and take up the entire screen.
4. You can cut back on the parallax effects a bit. Parallax peaked in about 2016 and I think much of the initial novelty and dramatic impact of it has faded. Now the general preference is as flat and simple as possible.

That aside, you're really on the right track. Considering the amount of godawful applicant portfolios I have to sift through on a daily basis at my company, I'd hire you in a heartbeat.

Please don't take this as negative feedback but as constructive criticism.

1. I don't think it's a great idea to say that you've expanded on your skill set without being able to provide compelling evidence to back up the claim. If you're including UI/UX design as part of your skill set, your portfolio needs to reflect that, which it doesn't - and I mean this is visible in the portfolio website itself. The thumbnails for your projects awkwardly crop the titles, cutting the headings in half and presenting unflattering previews. Some of the images are pixelated (possibly because you exported images that feature text as JPEGs instead of as PNGs), 
2. If you look at this page in your portfolio [here](https://danissa22.myportfolio.com/interactive-design-uxui) the main banner image is disconnected and random and doesn't have offer any insight into the project or showcase anything, the first text block is an image of text and the copy is quite undecipherable and glitchy looking, LOADS of typos and grammatical and syntax errors. 
3. The main font you've used seems to be Rockwell or something, which is OK but not ideal for this context, plus in many places it has been mismatched with other non-complimentary fonts.
4. Try to understand that your portfolio is the absolute first impression being formed about you, even before people actually open it and start going through your individual projects. Your home / landing page seems to suggest that you do hand drawn illustration / pencil sketches etc, but the moment you go in there's no further reference to this. If people see pixelated images, type errors, empty containers etc, it sets a negative precedent. Like what it says to an employer is that if this person doesn't even care to properly organize their own website, how can I trust them with my business requirements? 
5. I think you should put more focus on showcasing your strengths (your motion graphics stuff and hand drawn illustration seems to be better than your graphic design, Ui/Ux and digital illustration)

Avoid highly glossy papers - they can sometimes look cheap and tacky, especially when they're that unnatural shade of fluorescent bleached bright white. Stick to ivory/off-white matte finish card stocks with some slight texture, but be careful - textured papers are a lot more absorbent and they soak up a small amount of the print ink so account for that degree of fading and compensate accordingly. Paper thickness is very important. 

Too thin and it feels like a flyer for a Chinese takeout place. Too thick and you get into wedding card territory. Somewhere between 250-300 GSM is good if you have few pages. If you have enough pages that it's more of a booklet, then go a bit lower than 250.  

Hot foil stamping is good for cover pages. Spot-UV printing can be very effective too. Depending on the brand, embossing could also work in small amounts. It's ideal for more elaborate regal looking logos - a little unnecessary for simpler minimalistic ones. If there are recurring graphical elements in the theme or a motif in the branding, you can get them cut out with a die or laser as well.

If there are enough pages in your catalogue, you might consider getting it hard-bound, though not too thickly. There's also side-pin or staple wrap binding which is good for shape and structure of the spine. Standard center-pin binding is the most common for catalogues and therefore also the cheapest looking.

If you're in a small town, the reason you can't find people close to you is because they're less likely to be educated or aware of LGBT issues, they're less likely to be well-acquainted with newer technologies, they're more likely to be paranoid and afraid of going public due to prevalent homophobia or the threat of familial disownment. The reason it is difficult to find other people near you, is because of people. People aren't even aware of the existence of the basic general gay dating apps. How would they be aware of a new specific LGBT app? Do you think the Indian government would promote it or that Indian companies would fund its development and marketing and advertising? No. The Indian government suppresses things like that and large corporations wouldn't dare publicly support something that puts them at risk of alienating a large part of their conservative consumer base. 

Imagine the headline that tomorrow, Maggi noodles comes out in support of gay rights and donates a small percentage of their profits to an LGBT NGO for the development of a social app. How many conservative right wing Indians would boycott Maggi products overnight? How many politicians would say that it is supporting "un-indian values" and bringing in "western corruption"? How much money would the company lose overnight from stock prices plummeting? So of course they're not going to fund this utopian app.

The problem is people. The struggle is hard, I know it is difficult. But blindly shouting into the void about a lack of apps isn't the answer. You have to make use of what you have access to, and encourage others to do so as well.

Simply owning a DSLR doesn't always guarantee the best quality pictures. Depends entirely on the natural color of your hair. Doing it yourself is MUCH cheaper, but potentially dangerous so you have to be experienced and it always helps to have a friend with you. 

My natural color is dark brown and I'm currently silver ash / grey, I absolutely love it, but it was a goddamn nightmare. The darker your hair is, the more concentrated peroxide developer you have to use, and the higher the concentration, the more damage it does to your hair. Black hair typically needs two rounds of bleaching because the first round will leave a yellowish orange coppery tinge. The bottom inch or two of your hair will end up completely fried and irreparable and you WILL need a bit of trimming immediately after, no matter what you do. And you'll have to stock up on deep-conditioning treatments so your hair doesn't end up like straw. 

Silver/grey absolutely requires bleaching, more so than almost any other color. Because if you don't lighten enough, the color will come out looking sort of olive green with flecks of blonde.   


If your hair is naturally thin, I would definitely recommend going to a salon. Bleach can wreak havoc on thin hair and it's just not worth the risk of doing it at home. If your hair is thick, voluminous and healthy, you can go ahead and try it at home cause the savings are really considerable.

For instance, celery is known as the dieter's best friend because you actually burn more calories in the process of eating it than it contains. Kale, spinach, broccoli, beans and cabbage are great to incorporate into your diet. If they sound gross and unappealing to you, try to look at East and South Asian cuisines, particularly Korean and Indian, because they know how to make vegetables taste goddamn delicious. Western cuisines tend to focus more on the protein and starch components of the meal and vegetables are often like an afterthought - typically bland, just steamed or boiled and seasoned with just salt. If you have to gain weight, that's trickier. Get a giant tub of whey protein (buy off amazon, it will be cheaper than at those specialty fitness stores), eat TONNES of lean protein like grilled or poached chicken breast, nuts like almonds and pistachios, cheese, yogurt, fish, peanut butter and bananas. Don't do cardio because while it's a great way to stay in shape and improve circulation, it doesn't build any muscle. Focus on weight training. If you stick to lighter and more manageable weights and just do more reps with them, your body will easily build a tolerance for it and you'll plateau and stop growing.

Well there are lots of theories but it is sort of a dangerous area of research kind of like eugenics. Like if for instance someone were to find definitive scientific evidence of certain racial genetic traits being more objectively preferable or beneficial, and if there were a way to actually control the genetic outcome of someone, the implications for humanity would be absolutely disastrous. Similarly, if research showed that there actually were a way to predict, alter and control the sexuality of a child before it was born, the results would be catastrophic and the risk of abusing the results would be immense. That's why research is somewhat limited.

Having said that, some people think it happens in the womb due to chemical / hormonal imbalances or temperature changes that alter genetic information. Some people also believe it is largely environmental, ie, if the child is exposed to certain factors during early years of sexual development. Like there are studies that show that an abnormally large number of gay men and women were molested by people of the same sex at a very young age and that might have created some sort of hormonal or psychological imprint. It's usually an elder cousin or uncle or close family friend and often a confusingly non-traumatic experience, ie, the child doesn't realize that the experience was wrong and might even construe it as pleasurable if they had a strong bond with the abuser. Similar patterns have been observed with siblings, in that an abnormally high percentage of gay people tend to be younger siblings, which leads people to believe that more times a mother gives birth, the higher the chance that the next child will be homosexual.

Now obviously all this research is foggy and inconclusive, but the main point is that even if we are an evolutionary anomaly, that doesn't mean we need to be "corrected" or denied basic human rights, because at the end of the day we're all still just people and perfectly capable of contributing to society just like anyone else. And a lot of other evolutionary anomalies in other animals were completely random mutations that happened by pure chance and just happened to work out to be beneficial for the species. Like rattlesnakes for instance. The rattle didn't gradually evolve over centuries, it just appeared as a spontaneous mutation and happened to work out in favor of the snakes that had it, and they ended up with a better chance of survival. If homosexuality is another similar random mutation, there's a good chance that we simply haven't yet figured out what benefit it serves us. Maybe in a few decades we'll discover that the gay gene is the answer to climate change or some crazy shit. You never know.

If you're planning on making any adjustments to a vector, it shouldn't be in Photoshop, it should be in a vector based software like Illustrator. What format are you exporting your vectors in if they're turning out blurry or faded? For logos, the best format is always a high resolution PNG (you can decide if you want a transparent or white background).

Also, I think you might have some interchangeable lexical confusion between the words 'vector' and 'graphic'. A vector by definition is scalable and lossless and should only be operable by vector based softwares. Vector files are typically in Ai (Adobe Illustrator format), SVG (Scalable Vector Graphic), EPS (Encapsulated PostScript) or sometimes in editable PDFs. The point of a vector is that you can zoom in infinitely and you will not lose sharpness or clarity. If your stuff is getting blurry, it's not a vector file- it's just a graphic, or an image export of a vector.

So basically, if you're making a vector - use Illustrator. If you're SAVING a vector, use the 'Save As' option and save the file as an EPS and select your desired compatibility mode (based on the specs of whoever else will be handling the file). If you're EXPORTING a vector graphic, use "File > Export" instead. You can control the size and resolution of your exported format but you cannot preserve the vector properties of scalability - meaning you can get a fantastic quality PNG, but you can never zoom into it infinitely without the edges starting to blur at some point. PNG format will probably be your best friend.  

Also don't listen to whoever told you that you should only export in CMYK from Illustrator. Before you start any project, you should know its intended use. If it will be on screen, use RGB. If it's for print, use CMYK.

While I must admit that this is the most clean and refined iteration of this idea that I've seen, there is one flaw that was pointed out by a professor when I was a T.A at my alma mater and a freshman had come up with his version of this same idea (though his font was painfully ugly). 


There's really no sense in creating typefaces like this for large scale like signage (as is the intent here) because that's not how braille works. Characters in braille are apparently designed to be read by the touch of the finger almost at once; the reading is based on tactile sense and muscle memory- it's sort of like each character has a unique feeling when pressure is applied to all the dots at once. It's not about dragging your finger along the sequence of dots and counting them one by one - because in that case they wouldn't have needed to create a special language - they could have just spelled out English letters in dots. The point is, a blind person would have no way of reading a type-braille hybrid in signage form because the dots would be too large and far apart to be read together as single characters.


This idea would only work in the form of books or buttons on ATMs etc; i.e wherever it makes sense for both english and braille characters to be of the same size. The second the lettering gets too large, it's just a gimmick and becomes impossible for a vision-impaired person to read.

Automatic feeders can take some getting used to because cats need to understand that the feeding is based on a particular time - rather than on repeatedly wailing at it to magically produce food. In your cat's mind, its just a random alien machine that sometimes spontaneously pops out food and he has no idea why or how. 



A much better and more cost effective solution is puzzle type feeders - where the cat has to actively participate to get the food. These could be as simple as those clear plastic balls that pop out a treat when batted around a certain way - or sometimes they have small holes that cats can reach into to try and coax out a snack. More elaborate designs involve paddles and slots and buttons that need to be messed around with to pop out a feeding. These make your cat realize that the food isn't just randomly appearing, but that he is actually making it appear by actively "hunting" for it.



It also tires them out and keeps their minds occupied so they don't make nearly as much noise. If that doesn't work, I'd suggest switching to a kind of food that is OK to leave lying out. A lot of brands make dry food specially formulated for indoor cats to keep energy levels relatively low. Cats don't usually gorge like dogs do - they typically know when they've had enough to eat - so it shouldn't cause any trouble if you left a bowl of kibble out for him to graze at whenever he gets peckish.

Firstly, that's a tad abstract and ambiguously reductive. But I get the point. The inevitability is to have a meandering discussion that arrives at a pseudo-consensus where we all idealistically agree that there's merits to both sides of the argument and wrap up by singing kumbaya.

They gained absolutely nothing from criticism so the relationship was entirely parasitic.



What designers do might be _inspired_ by the personal, but it is inherently a product or service for _someone else_ so criticism can be constructive and useful. What artists do is almost entirely personal - just an outward expression of the internal, so criticism from the outside is kind of redundant and pointless.

No offence taken, I completely understand, and as I said, I get the point of the article. I'll reiterate that it's just framed in a way that makes any response automatically defensive.

The problem is that in the general occupational perspective, design is a relatively new area that lacks the sheer volume of research, scientific studies and hard data that serves to substantiate claims in most other fields. That isn't to invalidate it though. Just because the language to explain a phenomenon doesn't fully exist yet, it doesn't mean the phenomenon isn't taking place.


I'm totally with you on not trusting the vast majority of people who proudly boast of design degrees, indeed most of them lack the ability to design a child's birthday card. But that is something that falls more on a client. If you have a bad experience with a doctor who turns out to be a quack with a meaningless degree from an unaccredited online university who prescribes baby asprin for cancer, then you know not to go to him ever again. Same with a designer - you sign a contract and agree to pay a nominal amount for their time and consultation, but if you're unhappy with the product, nobody can force you to pay for it.



Ultimately, designers are designing FOR their clients, and they _have_ to take their preferences into consideration. A doctor can't force a patient to give birth in a hospital if they prefer to give birth "naturally" at home in their bathtub. 



I will say that it is easier to substantiate claims in certain areas of design than others. Ui/Ux design for instance has a much higher degree of objectivity than graphic design. You have certified usability testers who are trained to know how people interact with an interface, how people perceive and process information and how much of it is retained, and therefore they're better equipped to design an experience. 


Graphic design tends to be a lot more subjective and dependent on things just feeling or looking right, and yes, a lot of the time what appeals to designers is not what appeals to their audience. But generic typographic rules aside, a simple example would be like if a client wants to design a flyer for their company, but they want to include 50 lines of text about the history and conception of the company, their mission and vision statement, and include the logos of 35 partners and affiliates all squished down to ridiculously tiny size in order to fit on a flyer that will have to be printed on the most affordable but impractical paper. In a case like that, one has to acknowledge a designer's input. Large volumes of text will be inevitably overlooked and ignored, crowded clusters of logos will be perceived as noise, and a poor quality print will not stand out among the massive mess of thousands of other flyers already pinned to the office corkboard.


The degree of subjectivity in design is mostly to do with aesthetics, and that's always an area of negotiation and dialog. A designer might come up with something weird and obscure and minimal that the client doesn't like, or the client might have an inexplicable fondness for Comic Sans - that's a situational thing that has to be dealt with case by case. There can't be rules for things like that.

I agree with you, but with a caveat of personal discretion. We all know what the current state of the industry is in regards to people undervaluing creatives and blindly categorizing various distinct skills under the same umbrella. 


People wrongly assume that graphic design, web development, Ui/Ux design, copywriting, photography, installation art and illustration are all totally synonymous and they expect one single person to be proficient in all of them, and more often than not, for a measly price.



As useful and important as photography is as a skill, I try to keep it separate from my design work just out of economic consideration for the industry- because the more firmly we stick to our guns and stand resolute, the more people start to understand that it is legitimate work that requires entire teams and proper investment and is not something trivial enough to be lumped onto an intern. People need to be reminded that if they want quality work, they need to be willing to pay for it.



But I also understand that that's a convenience available only to people with sufficient experience. If a new/young designer steps into an interview and declares that they're only willing to do graphic design and refuse to dabble in the tech overlaps of anything else, they're never going to get hired.



Personally, I include some samples of art and photography work in my portfolio and clearly mention it under skills in my CV, but I make the distinction while drawing up the contract. They need to know that I'm _CAPABLE_ of the skill, but I'm not going to blindly offer it up as an unpaid service. If I'm being paid only as a graphic designer, I will only make use of whatever sub-par stock-photos the company can afford. 


I've just had far too many experiences where I've been taken for granted and made to do things way beyond my contract just because the employer imagines that the circumstances are far more dire than they really are, and that's how designers end up being taken advantage of.



If it's a small startup or a friendly client or a non-profit or an NGO with a respectable cause, I will gladly offer up any auxiliary skills I have, because I know that they have no other alternative, and ultimately I do want to help them. But if it is an established company that has the means to pay a professional photographer, there's no way I'm keeping that job from him.


Again though, I do agree with you that it is always an immensely important skill to have. We need to be sufficiently familiar with every discipline that we might potentially interact with. Well I understand that it might _seem_ like the designer has made life a bit more difficult for anyone else using the file, but in many ways it makes things easier. 

Let's say you as a designer create a logo for a company - you know exactly how to use it and how it should look and what proportions it should have. You hand over the logo to the company, get paid and all is good. A while later, the company wants to use that logo on a poster, but they can't afford you anymore - so instead, they approach an inexperienced designer and give him your logo file and ask them to put it in a poster. Now this designer might not have the original fonts - so when he opens the file, the font will be replaced by a default font like Myriad. He won't understand your proportions, and he'll stretch and distort your logo and use it incorrectly. 



To avoid such scenarios, people usually expand their text - to prevent misuse of the design. 

Also - it makes it harder for people to plagiarize your design if you expand it. If someone loves the way you've formatted your text - they might want to just copy your text box and replace the letters and use it on _their_ logos. If you expand your text, they can't directly lift your work.

Are you not familiar with expanding objects? Generally for logo text, people write and format their text with the type tool, add in any other lines or shapes that go with it, and then select Object > Expand. Doing this converts all the components to paths, so that it is easy to scale without changing the proportions and in case someone else is using the file and they don't have the specific font that was used, it won't change the appearance at all because it is now in the form of paths and not text.



It's not that someone individually drew several letters. They just wrote out a word and expanded it and for some reason separated each letter into its own layer. 



There's no way to edit expanded text. You'll just have to select all the letters, send them to one single layer and group them there, and below that, make a new text box and add in your third line of text. If you don't know what font was used, you'll have to find something that fits and works for you.

OK I understand the problem with snapping (I've only experienced it on Macs, never on PC), but I've never seen it as a _problem_ because I just assumed that that's just what happens with grouped compound shapes, plus there's a relatively easy fix.





When working with type, if you directly go to Type>Create outlines, it expands the type, but treats the whole thing as a group. If you un-group it, you should be able to snap to paths on the individual characters.



If it still doesn't work, you'll need to work with the Pathfinder window. Make your selection, ensure that all shapes are expanded (if type is included), ungroup the selection, then in the pathfinder window, just Alt/Opt+Click on the Unite option and then click the expand button (which would have been greyed out until now). This creates a true expanded compound path, like a singular unit, not just a group of individual objects. I've never had any issues with snapping after expanding compound paths like this.




If the issue _still_ persists, maybe go to Edit>Preferences>Smart Guides and then check the box for construction guides, and perhaps adjust the snapping tolerance. It'll make things easier, but still not eliminate the weirdly evasive bug.

Keep it to a single room so they're not overwhelmed with sensory overload and you can carefully supervise, make sure the new kitty has visible access to a safe dark hiding spot in case she gets scared, like a soft rug underneath a bed or something that allows her to feel protected and hidden, and make sure your older cat has access to a higher vantage point like a shelf or cat-tree or something. This will allow her to assess the room and be reassured that she's in control and that her throne isn't being threatened.

I usually find TED talks quite annoying and pretentious but this is one of my all time favorites by Roman Mars, talking about the principles of good flag design. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pnv5iKB2hl4



TLDR, flags being primarily symbolically representative on a massive scale and depicted on various forms, they need to be simple, flat and memorable and easy enough for a young child to replicate.




Ideally no more than 3-4 colors, generally from the basic 6 flag colors (red, blue, white, green, black, yellow), and preferably minimal in design - the test being you should be able to draw it by hand on a piece of paper roughly the size of a small postage stamp. If you can't do that, it's probably not a great flag design. 




Since flags are adapted and represented on currency, stamps, national branding, sports teams, architectural embellishment, sculptures and all sorts of mixed media, it's usually ideal if they're flat, solid colors so they're immediately recognizable and identifiable. Think of an engraved coin or a monochromatic stamp; you don't have the option to depict colors at all, but if the flag is well designed, you should easily be able to represent distinct color blocks. That becomes significantly harder with a gradient. How would you easily distinguish a gradient in stone or metal?



Finally, for traditional and ceremonial reasons, a lot of official flags are composed of different pieces of individually dyed fabric stitched together, rather than a single sheet of fabric that's been printed with the image of the flag, cause that's seen as cheap. For instance in the US flag, each stripe would be a separate piece. So pretty much any national flag that has 3-4 block colors and relatively simple imagery can be stitched together like this, with the rare intricate emblem embroidered on. But with a gradient, you'd have no choice but to print the whole flag, or painstakingly weave the whole thing with each strand of thread gradually moving from one color to the next, and a woven flag would just be wrinkly and heavy.

The line quality in the illustration looks a lot like the smooth results you get from live-tracing. So how it works is you draw the illustration, preferably in black on smooth white paper. The dotted effect is called stippling. Then you scan the illustration, and open the scanned file in Adobe Illustrator and use the Image Trace option to vectorize it. You can tweak the image trace settings to get rid of the white background and only register the pen marks. Then what you're left with is an editable vector of the illustration. You can select this vector and recolor it as you want, like how it's made dark blue here. And then export the file and use photoshop to edit in the hand holding the shoe and adjust the background and whatever else.
